title: Career Roadmap · Tool Room Technician
summary: A Tool Room Technician works with precision tools and equipment used to manufacture products in industrial settings. These tools may include dies, moulds, jigs, fixtures, cutting tools and gauges.

about.label: Industry
about.text: Manufacturing, precision engineering, automotive, aerospace, mould making and industrial tooling

about.label: Primary Workplaces
about.text: Tool rooms, machine shops, tool-and-die facilities, production plants and precision manufacturing units

about.label: Core Responsibility
about.text: Manufacture, maintain, repair and inspect tools, dies, jigs, fixtures, moulds and precision components

about.label: Key Skills
about.text: Engineering drawing, machining, metrology, fitting, CNC basics, tool maintenance and dimensional inspection

about.label: Suitable For
about.text: Students interested in practical mechanical work, precision manufacturing, machining and hands-on problem-solving

blocks.text: A Tool Room Technician works with precision tools and equipment used to manufacture products in industrial settings. These tools may include dies, moulds, jigs, fixtures, cutting tools and gauges.

The technician may operate conventional or CNC machines, perform fitting and finishing, inspect component dimensions, maintain tooling and support tool trials. The exact duties depend on whether the employer specialises in injection moulds, press tools, machining fixtures, automotive components or general tool-room work.

blocks.label: Important distinction
blocks.text: A tool room technician focuses on producing, maintaining and inspecting tooling. A CNC operator primarily operates machine tools for production, while a tool-and-die maker may have broader responsibility for designing, manufacturing, fitting and troubleshooting complex tools.

rows.text: Understand materials, dimensions and workshop safety
Identify wear, defects and tooling problems
Coordinate tooling jobs, maintenance and quality

blocks.text: This roadmap follows a typical three-year diploma structure. Actual subjects and workshop access vary by institution.
Year 1 — Mechanical and Workshop Foundations

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Develop fundamental mechanical engineering knowledge and safe workshop habits.
Core subjects:
Practical activities:

items.text: Practise marking, filing, sawing, drilling and deburring under supervision.
Identify common workshop tools and measuring instruments.
Use a steel rule, vernier caliper and micrometer under instruction.
Produce simple components to specified dimensions.
Maintain a workshop job sheet with measurements and inspection results.

blocks.label: Year 1 outcome
blocks.text: Understand workshop safety, basic manufacturing methods, engineering drawings and dimensional measurement.
Year 2 — Machining and Precision Measurement

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Develop practical machining and inspection skills.
Core subjects:
Practical activities:

items.text: Machine simple shafts, bushes and blocks using approved workshop procedures.
Calculate basic limits and fits for sample components.
Compare measured dimensions with specified tolerances.
Study the construction and purpose of simple jigs and fixtures.
Identify common cutting tools and their applications.

blocks.label: Year 2 outcome
blocks.text: Perform supervised machining, fitting and dimensional inspection while understanding precision requirements.
Year 3 — Tool Room Specialisation

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Prepare for entry-level work in tooling manufacture, maintenance and inspection.
Core subjects:
Practical activities:

items.text: Manufacture a simple fixture component from an engineering drawing.
Develop a CAD model of a basic jig or fixture.
Prepare a process plan for a small tooling component.
Inspect a finished component and document deviations.
Create a preventive-maintenance checklist for a sample tool.
Complete a supervised project involving machining, assembly and inspection.

blocks.label: Year 3 outcome
blocks.text: Demonstrate the practical foundation required for tool-room trainee, tooling technician and precision manufacturing support roles.

rows.text: Achieve required dimensions and surface quality
Check alignment, runout and dimensional variation
Ensure components fit and function correctly
Understand wear resistance and tooling performance
Support modern tooling and machining processes

blocks.text: The best tool stack depends on the employer's equipment and processes. Students should prioritise safe workshop competence and measurement accuracy before attempting advanced CNC or CAM tasks.
Project 1 — Precision-Fit Mechanical Component
Beginner

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Develop basic machining, fitting and inspection skills.
Build:

items.text: A simple shaft, bush or block from a supplied drawing.
A process sheet listing the machining and finishing steps.
A comparison of specified and measured dimensions.
A short report on errors and corrective actions.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: Drawing interpretation, workshop practice, measurement and quality control.
Project 2 — Drill Jig or Assembly Fixture
Intermediate

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Understand how tooling improves repeatability in manufacturing.
Build:

items.text: A CAD model of a simple drill jig or assembly fixture.
A component drawing with dimensions and tolerances.
An explanation of locating and clamping principles.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: CAD, fixture fundamentals, engineering drawings and process planning.
Project 3 — Tool Wear and Maintenance Study
Advanced

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Learn how tooling condition affects quality and production.
Build:

items.text: A record of tool condition using authorised workshop observations.
A checklist for cleaning, inspection and preventive maintenance.
A sample log of wear, defects and maintenance actions.
A comparison of component quality before and after maintenance.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: Tool maintenance, quality awareness, observation and technical reporting.
Project 4 — CAD-Based Tooling Component with Manufacturing Plan
Capstone

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Combine design interpretation, machining and inspection into one project.
Build:

items.text: A 3D model and manufacturing drawing for a simple tooling component.
A process plan listing operations, machines and inspection points.
A tooling and material selection rationale.
An inspection report and lessons-learned summary.

blocks.label: Skills demonstrated
blocks.text: CAD, manufacturing planning, precision measurement and quality documentation.
Projects involving machines, cutting tools, grinding or heat treatment must be carried out under appropriate workshop supervision and safety procedures.

After gaining experience, a tool room technician can specialise in:

blocks.label: Press Tool and Die Making
blocks.text: Manufacture and repair of stamping and forming dies.

blocks.label: Injection Mould Tooling
blocks.text: Manufacture, fitting and maintenance of moulds.

blocks.label: Jigs and Fixtures
blocks.text: Development and maintenance of production aids.

blocks.label: CNC Tool Room Operations
blocks.text: Precision machining and tool-room support using CNC equipment.

blocks.label: Precision Grinding
blocks.text: Producing accurate dimensions and surface finishes.

blocks.label: Tool Maintenance
blocks.text: Preventive servicing, repair and wear management.

blocks.label: Metrology and Inspection
blocks.text: Dimensional verification and measurement systems.

blocks.label: CAD/CAM Tooling
blocks.text: Digital modelling and machining preparation.

blocks.label: Tool Trial and Troubleshooting
blocks.text: Identifying tooling defects and production-quality issues.

blocks.label: Tool Room Supervision
blocks.text: Coordinating work orders, maintenance schedules and technicians.

A competitive entry-level profile should combine four areas.
Mechanical foundation
Practical manufacturing

By the end of the diploma, the student should aim to have:

items.text: The ability to interpret mechanical drawings.
Practical exposure to fitting and conventional machining.
Accurate use of basic precision measuring instruments.
Knowledge of dies, moulds, jigs and fixtures.
Basic CAD skills for mechanical components.
An understanding of tolerances and inspection requirements.
Two or three practical tooling or machining projects.
Internship or apprenticeship experience where available.
A CV tailored to tool room trainee, tool maintenance or precision manufacturing roles.

blocks.text: The most practical route is to begin as a tool room trainee, fitter trainee or machining trainee, gain supervised experience in manufacturing and inspection, and progressively specialise in dies, moulds, fixtures or CNC tooling.

For employability, prioritise a precision tooling project that includes a component drawing, manufacturing process plan, finished component, dimensional inspection report and documented deviations. This provides concrete evidence of practical skill rather than relying only on theoretical knowledge.
